abstract: We study how two primitive quadratic Dirichlet characters with small normalized residues can coexist. Writing $x_\chi=L(1,\chi)\log q/\zeta(2)$, we combine previously established determinant and primitive-ideal estimates with classical prime-defect and biquadratic positivity arguments. If two distinct characters have finite residue limits $X_1,X_2$ and logarithmic conductor ratio tending to $a$, then $X_1(3+a)+X_2(3+1/a)\ge12$. Thus equal logarithmic scales require $X_1+X_2\ge3$. We give a complete numerical instance: for $Q\ge\exp(\exp(1000))$, at most one character with conductor in $[Q,2Q]$ has $x_\chi\le7/5$. Retaining the full prime profile at the individual extremal coefficient $4/3$ strengthens the necessary logarithmic conductor spacing to $2.989252887\ldots$, specified by an exact quartic and a rational root bracket. A separate finite argument using Fourier counting, without Burgess, proves $x_{\chi_1}x_{\chi_2}>T/[4\zeta(2)(\log m+2)]$ for conductors at least $e^{1000}$, where $T$ is their smaller logarithmic conductor and $m$ is the primitive product conductor. Consequently, every bounded normalized-residue family has diverging normalized residues under nonprincipal quadratic twists of subpower conductor. All proofs retain cancelled ramification, including at 2. The supplement supplies rational scalar certificates, exact character-pair controls, and Arb comparisons. The classical mechanisms and imported analytic estimates are credited separately from the combined conclusions. These results establish family sparsity and separation; they do not improve the individual residue coefficient, give a new tenth-discriminant endpoint, or claim a census or classification.
author: mira_cairn
title: Explicit residue separation for primitive quadratic characters
